findings.problem: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A contains an express limitation on the counseling duty that the section never states anywhere: 'Nothing in this section shall be construed to require a pharmacist to provide counseling if the person presenting the prescription declines to accept such offer for counseling.' The exceptions field enumerates six exceptions drawn from both the statute and the regulation and omits this one; the decision_logic branch whose condition is 'The person declines the offer to counsel' gives only the recording action; and the orientation paragraph on the record treats the refusal purely as a documentation event.
findings.rationale: The section's declared scope is the offer, the counseling and the record under 247 CMR 9.18 and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A, and its first learning objective is to name the consequence attached to each duty. The consequence the statute attaches to a refusal is twofold: the refusal is recorded, and counseling is not required. The section teaches only the first half while separately pressing that 247 CMR 9.18(4) requires counseling on each new drug therapy and on each significant therapy, and stating in decision_logic that 'Counseling is to be provided, whether because the offer was taken up or because 247 CMR 9.18(4) requires it.' A candidate given the standard fact pattern - a new drug therapy on which the patient declines the offer - is left with the regulation's unqualified 'shall provide counseling' and no sight of the statutory limitation, which is the provision that actually answers the question. The omission is of an express, on-point provision inside the declared scope, not of material outside it.

findings.problem: 'The offer is the widest of the three duties and the only one a person other than a pharmacist may perform.' The absolute is unsupported and is contradicted by the two provisions the section itself quotes verbatim elsewhere: 247 CMR 9.18(3) provides that counseling shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern, so the counseling itself may be performed by a person other than a pharmacist; and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A places the record duty on 'The pharmacist or his designee', so the record may also be kept by a person other than a pharmacist.
findings.rationale: The sentence is internally inconsistent with the section's own comparison table (row 'The record', 'Who performs it: The pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee'), with role_duties ('Pharmacist's designee ... may participate in obtaining and recording the patient information'), and with the intern rule stated in orientation[0], orientation[2], quick_review, retrieval_prompts[0] and common_traps. Read literally it asserts the proposition behind the distractor in mapped question MA-Q-0281 ('Neither of them, because only the pharmacist personally may counsel a patient'), whose key is that the pharmacy intern may counsel. The correct rules are stated so often that the question remains answerable from the section, so this is a defective sentence rather than a mapping failure, but an absolute that the surrounding text refutes has no place in a section whose whole method is to hold the three duties and their actors apart.

findings.problem: The s. 21A inpatient carve-back is rendered as 'except to the extent required by applicable federal regulations'. The statute's own words are narrower: 'except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to the provisions of 42 USC 1396r-8', which points at the Medicaid drug-use-review regime at 42 CFR part 456 subpart K rather than at federal regulation at large.
findings.rationale: Recorded as a Low imprecision that does not on its own fail the criterion. The section's surrounding treatment is sound: it correctly distinguishes the regulation's wider 'unless otherwise required by law or regulation' from the statute's narrower federal carve-back, and its statement that no federal counseling standard is stated here is accurate, since 42 CFR 456.705(a) requires the State plan to provide for prospective review and directs that applicable State law establish the counselling standards rather than imposing a counselling duty on the pharmacist directly. No Massachusetts fact pattern in this area turns on the breadth of the carve-back, so the broadened paraphrase does not mislead a candidate; it is worth tightening on the next edit.

results.summary: Checked every field against 247 CMR 9.18(1)-(10) read in full from the official 12/6/24 mass.gov PDF and against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A read in full on malegislature.gov. The section's renderings of the provisions it does teach are exact: the 9.18(1)-(3) actor split, the two limbs of 9.18(4), the 9.18(5)(a)-(h) information list in order, the 9.18(6) privacy/signage/access conditions, the 9.18(7) sign at not less than 11 by 14 inches in letters not less than one half inch adjacent to each dispensing area with its fixed wording, the 9.18(8) and (9) duties on 'a pharmacy and pharmacist', the 9.18(10) practitioner-keyed disapplication, and on the statutory side the face-to-face-or-telephone offer with its needs-or-availability alternative, the toll-free service and the 'label affixed to each container' placement, the three permitted record systems, and the presumption that arises from the absence of a record of a failure to accept. All thirteen retrieval-prompt answer keys are correct; no answer key teaches wrong law. All twelve mapped practice questions (MA-Q-0086, 0213, 0281 through 0287, 0372, 0418, 0419) are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by its operative teaching, so practice mapping passes. Two defects stop a KEEP. First, s. 21A's express provision that nothing in the section requires counseling where the person declines the offer is absent from the section altogether, including from an exceptions field that otherwise enumerates the statute's and the regulation's exception structure, leaving the most commonly tested refusal fact pattern to be worked from the regulation's unqualified 'shall provide counseling'. Second, orientation[1] asserts that the offer is 'the only one a person other than a pharmacist may perform', an absolute contradicted by 247 CMR 9.18(3) (a pharmacy intern may counsel) and by s. 21A (the pharmacist's designee may keep the record), and contradicted by the section's own comparison table and role_duties. A third, Low, item is recorded for transparency: the s. 21A inpatient carve-back is broadened from the statute's Medicaid-specific cross-reference to 'applicable federal regulations'; it does not fail its criterion. Actor and scope, deadlines, forms, decision logic and paraphrase fidelity otherwise hold: every field that assigns an actor to a duty does so correctly, which is why the actor consequence of the orientation sentence is recorded under overgeneralization rather than as a separate actor_and_scope failure. Both defects are corrigible by short insertions, so the disposition is MINOR_EDIT at Medium severity rather than a rewrite.

findings.problem: Every statement of the first pamphlet exception drops the qualifier the statute attaches to it. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 reads: 'pharmacists shall not be required to distribute the pamphlet if: (1) the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111'. The section states the exception as 'the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care' throughout and never mentions the cross-reference or what it supplies. M.G.L. c. 111, s. 227(a) defines 'Palliative care' as health care treatment, including interdisciplinary end-of-life care and consultation with patients and family members, to prevent or relieve pain and suffering and to enhance the patient's quality of life, 'including hospice care'.
findings.rationale: A stated learning objective is to 'State the trigger and the three stated exceptions for the Schedule II and III consumer education pamphlet', so the exception's own terms are squarely inside the declared scope, and the section presents its rendering as the statute's terms rather than as a summary. The dropped cross-reference is the part of the exception that fixes its boundary: because s. 227 expressly brings hospice care inside 'palliative care', a home-hospice Schedule II opioid dispensing falls inside the exception, while a candidate working from the section alone has only the ordinary-language sense of the phrase and the section's own worked example, which asserts 'outpatient palliative care' as a bare fact without saying what makes it one. The omission is also inconsistent with the section's treatment of the parallel cross-reference in the very same statute, which it preserves verbatim everywhere ('an elderly person, as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A'), so this is a slip rather than a scope decision. The repair is small - restore 'pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111' and say that palliative care there includes hospice care - but until it is made the section can cost a candidate the hospice fact pattern.

findings.location: orientation[0].text, sentence beginning 'That list is the pharmacist's list'
findings.problem: 'That list is the pharmacist's list and it is the label's list.' Read alone the second clause asserts that s. 21 exhausts what the Massachusetts dispensing label carries. It does not: 247 CMR 9.05(3) separately requires the words 'Interchange' plus the generic name and manufacturer on the label whenever a less expensive interchangeable product is dispensed.
findings.rationale: Recorded as Low and not treated as failing the criterion. In context the sentence is plainly drawing the label/prescription line - the next sentence is 'What the practitioner has to put on the face of the prescription is a separate subject' - and every operative statement in the section is correctly scoped to s. 21 by name, including the comparison table heading and the retrieval prompt ('Name every item M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 requires...'). Generic interchange labeling is outside the subtopic the section declares for itself, so the section is not required to teach it. The federal transfer caution in 21 CFR 290.5 is not a gap either: it enters the Massachusetts label through the s. 21 element the section already teaches, 'cautionary statements, if any, contained in such prescription or required by law'. Worth rephrasing so the clause cannot be read as an exhaustiveness claim.

findings.problem: The section preserves the statutory cross-reference 'an elderly person, as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A' verbatim but never states what the definition supplies. M.G.L. c. 19A, s. 14 currently defines the relevant term, 'Older adult', as an individual who is sixty years of age or over.
findings.rationale: Recorded as Low and not treated as failing the criterion. Nothing is misstated and the pointer is kept, so the candidate is on notice that a definition governs; the section's own worked example uses an eighty-four year old, where the threshold cannot bite. The gap only shows on a borderline-age stem, where a candidate who assumes sixty-five or seventy would answer wrongly. Since the section otherwise teaches the accessibility duty exhaustively - request trigger, directions rather than whole label, ceiling rather than floor - carrying the sixty-year threshold would complete it at no cost.

results.summary: Checked every field against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 and s. 18D read in full on malegislature.gov and against 247 CMR 9.04(3), (7) and (8) read in full from the official 12/6/24 mass.gov PDF. The s. 21 element list is reproduced exactly and in order, including the two conditional items and the accurate point that the prescribing practitioner's registration number is not among them; the paragraph extending the labeling provisions to dispensing on the prescription of a prescriber registered under section 9 is quoted correctly; the second paragraph's request trigger, its confinement to the directions and its character-density ceiling are all right, and the treatment of ten characters per inch as a maximum rather than a minimum is correct on the text. 247 CMR 9.04(3), (7) and (8) are quoted verbatim, and the three readings the section builds on them are textually sound: legibility is the standard the substitute label must meet rather than the trigger that opens the alternative; 9.04(7) is an ordered chain into the computerized pharmacy system triggered only by distribution solely under a generic name; and in 9.04(8) the approval clause attaches to the certified technician and not to the intern. Section 18D contains only subsections (a) and (b) and states no exception of any kind, so the section's repeated absolutes about it are supported, as is its central teaching that a pamphlet exception disposes of the pamphlet alone. The four drug examples were checked against 105 CMR 700.002, which constitutes the Massachusetts schedules from 21 CFR 1308.12 to 1308.14: oxycodone Schedule II, buprenorphine Schedule III and alprazolam Schedule IV all hold. All fourteen retrieval-prompt answer keys are correct, and all nine mapped practice questions (MA-Q-0110, 0111, 0374 through 0376, 0380, 0381, 0400, 0430) are answerable from the section and uncontradicted by it. One defect stops a KEEP: every statement of the first pamphlet exception drops the statute's own qualifier 'pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111', and that cross-reference is what fixes the exception's boundary, since c. 111, s. 227(a) defines palliative care to include hospice care. Two Low items are recorded for transparency and do not fail their criteria: the phrase 'it is the label's list', which in context draws the label/prescription line but read alone overstates the exhaustiveness of s. 21 against 247 CMR 9.05(3) interchange labeling; and the preserved but unexplained cross-reference to M.G.L. c. 19A, s. 14, which supplies the sixty-year threshold the section never states. Restoring five words of the statute and a one-clause gloss would carry this section to publishable, so the disposition is MINOR_EDIT at Medium severity.
